positions.as_written: Compare the lateral side, where the popliteus tendon interrupts the attachment and the meniscus is free over that segment.
Expect an effusion with a deep injury and not necessarily with a superficial one.
Read a meniscotibial detachment as a separation rather than a tear, because the treatment follows the anatomy: peripheral tissue in a vascular zone reattaches.
Preserve the meniscal attachment where an approach crosses it.
Treat it as the structure that converts a meniscus from a free spacer into a loaded wedge.
Assess the meniscal attachment when planning any medial opening.
Consider reattachment rather than excision for peripheral detachment, because the tissue is vascular and the anatomy supports healing.
Document whether an injury is deep, superficial or both, since the three behave differently and the examination can separate them.
Avoid treating the posteromedial border as a dividing line between this ligament and the corner.
